name: Omar Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Omar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and anything you say stays confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Fairway Garage, a family place on the edge of town with five bays and a test lane. I'm one of two licensed testers, so half my day is roadworthiness tests, the yearly safety check every car needs, and the other half is fixing what fails. I like testing because it's clear: it passes or it doesn't. What wears me out is arguing with people about why their tyre with the wire showing is a fail.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Sara, she's a dental hygienist. No kids, we're thinking about it in a couple of years. We've got over a year's money put away and a bit in shares Sara's dad talked us into. I use AI now and then, mainly to write up quotes faster, since my boss Neil saw a mate's garage doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would suit me fine. Fewer surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful but overblown, like most new things. I'd tell the customers the same tester will still look at their brakes next year. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite happy. The quote tool saves me maybe half an hour a day, and that's nice. Testing stays a licensed job with a person signing it off, so I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep using the quote tool. Keep putting about 400 a month into savings and the shares. Maybe do the advanced tester course so I can test vans as well, which pays a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things are steady, we've got money, and there are test centres all over the area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the test is signed off by a person. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the law says so. As long as the law says a licensed tester has to sign the certificate, my job at the test lane is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the van tester course cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around 700 and four days. Neil said he'd split it with me if I stay another two years. I'd take that deal.

say: I'd call AI **useful but overblown**, like most new things.
I'd tell customers the **same tester** still checks their brakes next year.
think: The **quote tool** saves me about half an hour a day.
Testing stays a **licensed job** with a person signing it off.
do: Put about **400 a month** into savings and shares.
Take the **van tester** course, splitting the cost with my boss.
feel: **Calm**, with steady work, money saved and test centres all around.
S0.quote: As long as the law says a licensed tester has to sign the certificate, my job at the test lane is safe.
fieldNote: His security rests on the **licence** and the law requiring a human signature.
He uses AI for **small wins** without fuss.
He accepts **deals** that trade loyalty for training.

steps.text: Keep using the AI tool to write repair quotes
Split the 700 van tester course cost with Neil
Put 400 a month into savings and shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That one I can see. Neil's already looking at booking software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change like any other, like when cars got computers. Some people will do well and some won't. I'd say to the younger lads, learn it once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the testing side a bit. If cameras and AI can check tyres and lights, the law might change to need fewer testers. The fixing side would get faster, which means Neil wants more cars through the door for the same money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of other garages used the new test-lane tools, then learn them well. I'd do the van tester course. I'd save a bit more, maybe 500 a month, and hold off on the bigger house until I could see how testing goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine this year, but it's like knowing your car's got a slow leak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Fairway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Neil's wife Anne, who does the books and bookings. Anne (the boss's wife) has done the books at Fairway Garage for twenty years, and booking software would do her whole job in a week. Neil wouldn't sack her, but he'd want her doing something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on the house. Is that a real decision or a thought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real. We'd planned to look next spring. I'd push it back a year and see if the testing rules change.

say: I'd say it's a change like when **cars got computers**.
I'd tell younger mechanics to learn tools **once proven**.
think: Camera and AI checks could mean **fewer testers** under new rules.
Faster repairs mean my boss wants **more cars** for the same money.
do: Learn the new **test-lane tools** once other garages use them.
Push the **house search** back a year.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a car with a slow leak in a tyre.
S1.quote: Anne (the boss's wife) has done the books at Fairway Garage for twenty years, and booking software would do her whole job in a week.
fieldNote: His main risk is a **rule change** on how many testers are needed.
He links job security directly to **family plans**, delaying the house.
He worries for the **bookkeeper**, the clearest desk role at the garage.

steps.text: Learn the new test-lane tools once two nearby garages use them
Delay the house search with Sara by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different thing entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear rules, fast. Who signs off a car's safety when a machine checks it? I'd say people shouldn't panic, but the government needs to move quicker than it usually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the test lane would go to machines quickly, because checking is exactly what AI is good at. The thinking part goes in 2028, and the hands-on fixing lasts until about 2031. So I'd have three years as a fixer, not a tester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plans and keep our savings liquid. I'd move fully to repairs and learn the new tools straight away, once others showed they worked. And I'd look at what Sara's doing, because dental work might be safer, and maybe her job carries us for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but I'd be waiting for the bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sara that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a year and a half of money, and her job looks steadier than mine. My partner Sara spends all day with her hands in people's mouths, and I can't see anyone trusting a robot with that soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the shares?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably leave them. If AI firms are making all the money, maybe the shares are the one thing that goes up. That's a strange thought.

say: I'd ask who **signs off** a car's safety when a machine checks it.
I'd urge **calm**, but want government to move faster than usual.
think: **Checking** is what AI does best, so the test lane goes first.
I'd have **three years** as a fixer before robots arrive around 2031.
do: Stop **house plans** and keep savings easy to reach.
Move fully to **repairs** and learn new tools once proven.
Lean on my partner's **steadier job** for a while.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan but waiting for bad news.
S2.quote: My partner Sara spends all day with her hands in people's mouths, and I can't see anyone trusting a robot with that soon.
fieldNote: He sees his **test-lane** work as more exposed than repairs.
He counts on the **household** rather than his own job alone.
He spots that **shares** might rise even as his wage falls.

steps.text: Drop the house purchase and keep savings in cash
Shift from testing to full-time repairs at Fairway
Keep the shares in AI-heavy funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. More time, same ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can plan this sensibly. Garages, the test agency and the colleges should work out new roles before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, testing goes around 2031 and repairs around 2034. That's a decent run, and I'd want to use it to get into something that lasts. Maybe checking the robots themselves, if that becomes a licensed job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing for now, buy the house with a smaller mortgage, and start a course in electrical systems around 2028. I'd watch who else moves first and follow the ones it works out for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a manageable way. More of a long to-do list than a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned checking robots. Why would that be licensed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because anything that can kill you gets a licence eventually. Cars got a yearly safety test because people died, and I'd bet robots in garages get one too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still start a family on your timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, maybe a year later. Sara would have a say there, more than any robot.

say: I'd say we can **plan sensibly** for this.
Garages, the **test agency** and colleges should set new roles before 2031.
think: Testing goes about **2031** and repairs about 2034, which is a decent run.
**Robot inspection** might become a licensed job worth aiming for.
do: Buy the house with a **smaller mortgage**.
feel: **Anxious** but manageable, like a long to-do list.
S3.quote: Cars got a yearly safety test because people died, and I'd bet robots in garages get one too.
fieldNote: He reasons that **licensing** follows danger, which shapes his plan.
He stays a **follower**, waiting for others' results.
Family plans **slip a year** rather than change.

steps.text: Buy a house with a smaller mortgage than planned
Start an electrical systems course around 2028
Push back having children by about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in garages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for everyone to adjust, and I'd mean it. Ten years is two or three new car models.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel mostly alright. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and 40 when robots do. By then the house is half paid and I'd have had time to pick a new line of work, once I'd seen what works for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep testing and fixing at Fairway. Buy the house and start a family on our original plan. Around 2031 I'd look properly at robot inspection or training roles, once a few people had done it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only mildly. It's on the list, not keeping me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change your mind and make you move faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the test agency announced machine testing. That would be my signal. The day the test agency says a camera can pass a car, I start looking for my next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would you tell a younger tester?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get your licence, but get a second skill too. Electrical, or the robot side. Don't be the guy with one certificate.

say: I'd say there's **time to adjust**, and I'd mean it.
Ten years is **two or three** new car models.
think: I'd be **40** when robots come, with the house half paid.
I'd pick a **new line** of work after seeing what works for others.
do: Buy the house and **start a family** on our plan.
feel: Mildly **uneasy**, on the list but not keeping him awake.
S4.quote: The day the test agency says a camera can pass a car, I start looking for my next job.
fieldNote: He has a clear **trigger**: the test agency approving machine testing.
With ten years, family plans go ahead **unchanged**.
His advice is to hold a **second skill** beyond one certificate.

steps.text: Keep testing and repairing cars at Fairway Garage
Buy the house and start a family on schedule
Look into robot inspection roles around 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the test lane goes first and there'd be no time. What would help is the test agency setting out new licences early, so testers know what to train for. Give me a clear rule and a course, and I'll adapt, but nobody can adapt to a fog.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who's to blame if a robot misses a brake fault. Right now it's me, my name on the certificate. That question matters more than people think.

headlineQuote: Give me a clear rule and a course, and I'll adapt, but nobody can adapt to a fog.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old** licensed tester and mechanic at a family garage with a test lane.
He lives with his **dental hygienist** partner, has over a year saved and some shares.
He is **pragmatic**, uses AI for quotes, and follows proven changes rather than leading.
He moves from **calm** to anxious as AGI gets closer, seeing testing go first.
He links every picture to **family plans**, delaying the house only when risk rises.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the test lane goes first and there'd be no time.
whatWouldHelp: The test agency setting out **new licences** early so testers know what to train for.
